new.title: Stroll under the columns of the old Fish Market
new.desc: The city architect Jan-Robert Calloigne built this colonnade of Tuscan columns around an open square in 1821, and the stone fish counters date from 1852. Fish was sold in the open air on the Markt until 1745, before it moved here.
new.tip: Come on a morning from Wednesday to Saturday, when fishmongers still sell from the stone slabs. Later in the day the colonnade fills with painters and craft stalls.

new.title: Look up at the tapestries in Sint-Salvator's Cathedral
new.desc: Bruges' oldest parish church only became its cathedral in 1834, and its 99 metre tower got its neo-Romanesque top from Robert Chantrell after a fire in 1839. Inside hang Brussels tapestries woven by Jasper van der Borcht in 1731 for the lost Sint-Donaas cathedral on the Burg.
new.tip: Entry to the church is free. Listen out for the big organ, first built by Jacobus Van Eynde around 1719 and still used for concerts.

new.title: Have breakfast where an archduke was held captive
new.desc: The Craenenburg on the Markt takes its name from a resident recorded here in 1305, and in 1488 the rebellious burghers of Bruges locked up Archduke Maximilian of Austria in this house. Today it is a classic Belgian-French café with a front-row view of the Belfort.
new.tip: It opens at 8 every day and at 7 on Wednesdays, when the weekly market fills the square. Grab a window table for coffee before the crowds arrive.

new.title: Queue with the locals for gelato at Da Vinci
new.desc: This ice cream parlour on Geldmuntstraat has been scooping gelato for Bruges since the hot summer of 1995. It is the place locals send you when you ask for ice cream, and the line on the pavement in summer is part of the ritual.
new.tip: Go in the early evening, after the day trippers have left. The queue moves faster than it looks.

new.title: Pick a picnic cheese at the Diksmuids Boterhuis
new.desc: Founded in 1933, this cheese and fine meats shop on Geldmuntstraat is one of the old food institutions of the centre. Its counters are stacked with Belgian and Flemish cheeses, hams and sausages.
new.tip: Ask for a taste of a few local cheeses before you buy, then take your picnic to the benches of the Koning Albert I-park or along the Dijver.

new.title: Follow cocoa from the Maya to the praline at Choco-Story
new.desc: This chocolate museum on Sint-Jansplein tells the story of cocoa from Central America to the Belgian praline, invented in Brussels in 1912. The visit ends with a demonstration and a taste of freshly made chocolate.
new.tip: Book a time slot online, as it can turn away walk-ins on busy days. It is a good plan B for a wet afternoon with children.

new.title: Peek into the church from the Gruuthuse oratory
new.desc: The lords of Gruuthuse grew rich on the right to tax gruut, the herb mix used to flavour beer before hops, and turned their storehouse into a palace. In 1472 Louis of Gruuthuse added a private chapel with a window straight into the Church of Our Lady next door, so his family could attend mass without leaving home.
new.tip: Look for the bell from around 1245, the oldest in Flanders, and the painted terracotta bust of the young Charles V. A combined ticket with the Church of Our Lady museum saves money.

new.title: Taste a sour red at Bourgogne des Flandres
new.desc: The Van Houtryve family has brewed since 1765, but brewing stopped in Bruges in 1957 and the beer was made near Brussels for decades. In 2015 Bourgogne des Flandres came home to a brewery a few steps from the Dijver, where its red-brown blend of young beer and lambic is made again.
new.tip: A visit with a beer tasting costs about 16 euros. On weekend evenings there is a blending session where you mix your own glass.

new.title: Try butter truffles at Sukerbuyc
new.desc: Sukerbuyc on Katelijnestraat is one of the oldest chocolatiers in Bruges and still makes its pralines, bars and butter truffles in its own workshop. It sits on the walk between the Church of Our Lady and the Begijnhof.
new.tip: It is open every day from 10 to 6. Buy a small mixed box and eat it by the water at the Begijnhof bridge.

new.title: Circle the Minnewater past the old powder tower
new.desc: The Lake of Love is really a 13th-century buffer basin that regulated the water flowing into the city, and until 1784 the barge to Ghent moored here. The brick Poertoren on its bank stored the town's gunpowder, and legend says it marks the grave of Minna, a girl who died fleeing a forced marriage.
new.tip: Walk the loop through the Minnewaterpark on the far bank, which most visitors skip. At dusk the light on the water is lovely.

new.title: Hunt for treasures at the Dijver flea market
new.desc: On weekends and public holidays from mid-March to mid-November, second-hand dealers and craftspeople set up under the trees along the Dijver canal. Expect old prints, lace, silverware and curiosities in one of the prettiest settings in town.
new.tip: It runs roughly from 10 to 6. Come early for the best finds and pair it with a look at the canal from the Sint-Bonifaciusbrug nearby.

new.title: Shop the Saturday market on 't Zand
new.desc: Every Saturday morning the big square of 't Zand and the neighbouring Beursplein fill with the city's largest market: vegetables, cheese, flowers, clothes and household goods. It is where Bruges families do their weekly shopping.
new.tip: It runs from about 8 to half past one. Arrive early for the food stalls, and grab a hot snack from one of the vans.

new.title: Step into the Jerusalem Chapel of the Adornes family
new.desc: The Genoese merchant family Adornes built this odd private chapel in 1428 and 1429 as a copy of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. In the centre lies the tomb of Anselm Adornes and his wife Margriet; Anselm was buried in Scotland, but his heart was brought here in 1483.
new.tip: The ticket also covers the lace museum in the Adornes mansion. It is open Monday to Saturday.

new.title: Find the baroque surprise inside Sint-Anna church
new.desc: The neighbourhood church was rebuilt between 1611 and 1621 after the old one was sold off in the Reformation troubles. Its plain Gothic shell hides such a rich baroque interior that locals call it the salon church of Bruges, with a 1670 pulpit and a huge Last Judgement by Hendrik Herregouts.
new.tip: Combine it with the Jerusalem Chapel and the Folklore Museum, all within a few minutes' walk.

new.title: Admire the Jesuit pulpit of Sint-Walburga
new.desc: The Jesuit lay brother Pieter Huyssens designed this baroque church, built from 1619 to 1643; its tower was never finished for lack of money. The oak pulpit by Artus Quellinus the Younger counts as the finest in Bruges, and a 24 metre white marble communion rail runs across the choir.
new.tip: The church hosts concerts, so check for evening performances. Sit in the nave for a moment to take in the light on the marble.

new.title: Sit in the garden where Guido Gezelle grew up
new.desc: The priest and poet Guido Gezelle, Flanders' best-loved 19th-century writer, was born in this small house on the Rolweg and spent his youth here. The shady garden with its organic vegetable beds is now a quiet corner of the Sint-Anna district, with a Jan Fabre sculpture by the entrance.
new.tip: The garden is open most days, but the museum rooms with his desk and manuscripts only open on the second Sunday of the month.

new.title: Play old games at the Folklore Museum
new.desc: A row of 17th-century workmen's cottages on Balstraat recreates everyday Bruges life of around 1900, with a classroom, pharmacy, tailor, grocer and sweet shop. Children can practise handwriting, weigh coffee and try on hats, and a folk games case comes out in good weather.
new.tip: On Thursday afternoons a sweet maker boils candy in the shop. End with a drink in the museum's own inn, De Zwarte Kat.

new.title: Have coffee at De Windmolen by the ramparts
new.desc: This corner café at the end of Carmersstraat sits right below the windmills on the Kruisvest, with a terrace looking out over the canal. It is a neighbourhood spot where coffee comes with a little treat and the decor nods to the mills outside.
new.tip: Hours are short and it is usually closed on Saturdays, so plan a weekday morning stop on your walk along the windmills.

new.title: Eat spaghetti on the terrace of L'Estaminet
new.desc: This old-style café faces the Koningin Astridpark, a quiet green square east of the Burg. Locals come for simple plates such as its spaghetti and croque monsieur.
new.tip: On a sunny day grab a table on the terrace by the park. Afterwards take a turn around the park's pond and bandstand.

new.title: See the art of the Burgundian court in Sint-Jakobskerk
new.desc: First built around 1240, Sint-Jakob was greatly enlarged in 1459 when the Dukes of Burgundy, who lived at the nearby Prinsenhof, became its patrons. Rich merchants filled it with paintings and tombs, and the interior was redone in baroque style around 1700.
new.tip: It is one of the least crowded big churches in town. Pair it with a walk past the Prinsenhof gate on Noordzandstraat.

new.title: Find the Medici bank in Hof Bladelin
new.desc: Pieter Bladelin, treasurer of the Order of the Golden Fleece, built this city palace in 1435. From 1466 it housed the Bruges branch of the Medici bank, run by Tommaso Portinari, and its walled courtyard with box hedges and a Gothic tower still feels Florentine.
new.tip: If the gate is open, step into the courtyard to see the Gothic tower. The street front on Naaldenstraat is worth the detour anyway.

new.title: Pay respects to Memling in Sint-Gillis church
new.desc: This brick church in the quiet Sint-Gillis quarter dates from around 1240 and took its present hall shape in the 1460s and 1470s. The painters Hans Memling, Lanceloot Blondeel and Pieter Pourbus were all buried here, though their graves are lost.
new.tip: Look for the 1783 painting by Jan Garemijn of a local man ransomed from slavery in Barbary. The streets around the church are among the most peaceful in town.

new.title: Visit the miraculous Madonna of the Potterie
new.desc: This hospital on the Potterierei is recorded from 1269 and still cares for the elderly today, with a few Augustinian sisters on site. Its church, made rich and baroque by pilgrims to a 13th-century miraculous statue of Mary, is now a small museum full of silver, tapestries and paintings.
new.tip: Walk here along the Langerei and Potterierei canals, the quietest waterside route in town. It is rarely busy.

new.title: Order a beer stew at Cambrinus
new.desc: This beer brasserie just north of the Markt has a thick menu of Belgian brews and a kitchen that cooks with them, from beer stews to set menus built around Trappist beers.
new.tip: Book ahead for dinner. Ask the staff to pair a beer with your main course.

new.title: Drink a Trappist under the roses at Café Rose Red
new.desc: Since 2010 the Veireman family has run this candlelit beer bar with rows of red roses hanging from its beamed ceiling. The list runs to well over a hundred beers with a focus on Trappists, and a few draughts change regularly.
new.tip: Ask about the aged bottles from the cellar. It is a calm alternative to the busier bars on the Markt.

new.title: Catch a show at the Royal City Theatre
new.desc: The Stadsschouwburg opened in 1869 with a design by Gustave Saintenoy inspired by Garnier's Paris Opera. Its red velvet hall with about 700 seats and a monumental chandelier is one of the best preserved city theatres in Europe.
new.tip: Check the programme of Cultuurcentrum Brugge for theatre, dance and concerts. Arrive early to see the foyer.

new.title: Visit James Ensor's home above the shell shop
new.desc: The painter James Ensor lived and worked in this Ostend house from 1917 until his death in 1949. On the ground floor his uncle and aunt's shell and souvenir shop has been kept as it was, and upstairs is the Blue Salon where he painted and received guests.
new.tip: Since 2020 a modern visitor centre next door introduces his masks and carnival world before you climb into the house.

new.title: Board the tall ship Mercator in Ostend
new.desc: This three-masted barquentine was built in Scotland in 1932 as the training ship of the Belgian merchant navy. On one voyage it brought back a moai statue from Easter Island, and since 1964 it has been a museum ship in the heart of Ostend.
new.tip: Explore the cabins and the galley below deck. It is a short walk from the station.

new.title: Meet Delvaux's dreamy women in Sint-Idesbald
new.desc: The surrealist Paul Delvaux built a studio in Sint-Idesbald in 1951, and a fisherman's cottage nearby now holds the world's largest collection of his work. Besides his moonlit nudes and stations, you will find his collection of model trams and trains.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk in the dunes behind Sint-Idesbald and a ride on the coast tram.
new.q: Paul Delvaux Museum, Paul Delvauxlaan 42, Koksijde

new.title: Follow one soldier's story at the In Flanders Fields Museum
new.desc: The museum fills the upper floor of Ieper's Cloth Hall, which was shelled to ruins in the First World War and rebuilt by 1962. A poppy bracelet with a chip lets you follow the personal stories of four people through the war in the Westhoek.
new.tip: Pay a little extra to climb the belfry for a view over the town and the old battlefields. Then walk to the Menin Gate for the evening Last Post.
new.q: In Flanders Fields Museum, Grote Markt 34, Ieper

new.title: Stand among the graves of Tyne Cot
new.desc: With almost 12,000 burials, Tyne Cot near Passendale is the largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the world. Designed by Sir Herbert Baker, it has its Cross of Sacrifice built on a German pillbox, and its back wall lists nearly 35,000 soldiers with no known grave.
new.tip: Start in the small visitor centre, where the names of the dead are read aloud. Entry is free.

new.title: Learn how Nieuwpoort flooded the front in 1914
new.desc: In October 1914 the Belgians opened the sluices at the Ganzepoot in Nieuwpoort and flooded the IJzer plain, stopping the German advance. The 1938 King Albert I Memorial stands above the sluices, and since 2014 a visitor centre beneath it tells the story.
new.tip: Walk the circular gallery on top of the monument for a view over the sluices and the polders. Bring a jacket, it is windy up there.

new.title: See the platform of the giant gun Lange Max
new.desc: At Leugenboom near Koekelare, the Germans installed the Lange Max, then the largest gun in the world, which first fired on Dunkirk some 45 kilometres away on 27 June 1917. The museum shows the remains of the gun platform and the underground bunkers.
new.tip: It is a good stop on a drive between Diksmuide and the coast. Combine it with the Käthe Kollwitz statues at Vladslo.

new.title: Walk the cratered ground of Hill 60
new.desc: This low rise south-east of Ieper changed hands again and again in the First World War, and miners tunnelled beneath it to blow it apart. The ground is still pitted with craters, and the memorial to the 1st Australian Tunnelling Company carries bullet marks from the Second World War.
new.tip: Entry is free and open all day. Stay on the paths, as many soldiers still lie beneath the site.

new.title: Read the stories at Lijssenthoek Military Cemetery
new.desc: From 1915 to 1920 this hamlet near Poperinge was the largest evacuation hospital area behind the Ypres Salient, and the cemetery grew with every soldier who died of his wounds. A visitor centre beside the graves tells the stories of nurses, doctors and patients.
new.tip: Entry is free and the site is open daily. Cycle here from Poperinge along the quiet hop-field lanes.

new.title: Have a coffee in the Art Deco Brasserie du Parc
new.desc: On the Marie-Joséplein near the Kursaal, this brasserie keeps an authentic Art Deco interior in a hotel building from 1929, protected as one of the few Art Deco hotels left in Ostend. Artists, business people and locals mix here from breakfast to dinner.
new.tip: It opens early, at half past seven. Sit inside on a grey day for the full interwar atmosphere, outside in summer for the terrace.

new.title: Work through the beer list at 't Botteltje in Ostend
new.desc: This beer café on Louisastraat, with a small hotel upstairs, is the Ostend address for Belgian beer lovers. It has a long bottle list and a changing line-up of draught beers.
new.tip: Ask the staff what is new on tap. It closes for a few weeks in late summer and early spring, so check before you go.

new.title: Drink a Wipers Times inside Ieper's ramparts
new.desc: Since 2014 the Kazematten brewery has brewed beer in the old vaulted casemates under Ieper's ramparts near the Lille Gate. Its Wipers Times beers are named after the satirical newspaper British soldiers printed in the ruined town.
new.tip: Book a tour through the brewery's website, and finish on the terrace by the moat.
new.q: Brouwerij De Kazematten, Houten Paard 1, Ieper

new.title: Spend Saturday afternoon at the Struise brewery
new.desc: De Struise Brouwers are among Belgium's best-known craft brewers, famous for dark, strong beers such as Pannepot. Their brewery and tasting room are in the village of Oostvleteren, a few kilometres from the Westvleteren abbey.
new.tip: The tasting room only opens on Saturdays from 2 to 6 pm. Plan it with a stop at In de Vrede across the fields.

new.title: Eat eel at Siphon where the canals cross
new.desc: This polder restaurant on the Damse Vaart, just outside Damme, has served fresh eel as its house speciality for as long as anyone remembers. It takes its name from the siphon where the canals cross, deep in the poplar-lined countryside.
new.tip: Cycle out from Bruges via Damme and book ahead. It has long closing periods, so check the dates on its website first.

new.title: Lunch on the island in Ostend's Maria Hendrikapark
new.desc: Het Koninginnehof sits on an island in the largest pond of the 37 hectare Maria Hendrikapark, a short walk from Ostend station. Its huge terrace and self-service restaurant draw families for a simple lunch, with rowing boats and pedal cars for hire alongside.
new.tip: Rent a rowing boat after lunch. Check the online calendar, as hours change with the season.

new.title: Climb the cobbles of the Kemmelberg
new.desc: At 154 metres, the Kemmelberg is the highest point of West Flanders and its steep cobbled climb often decides the Gent-Wevelgem race. It was fiercely fought over in 1918, and a French memorial topped by a statue the locals call the Angel stands near the summit.
new.tip: Walk or cycle up from Kemmel village, but take care on the cobbles in the wet. A Cold War NATO bunker on the hill now opens as a visitor centre.

new.title: Watch the penitents carry their crosses through Veurne
new.desc: Every last Sunday of July since 1644, Veurne holds its Procession of the Penitents. Some 400 anonymous penitents in brown hooded habits carry heavy wooden crosses, between biblical scenes acted by hundreds of townspeople and explained by angels in old Dutch.
new.tip: It starts in the afternoon, around half past three. Find a spot along the route early and watch in respectful silence.

new.title: Learn how hops are grown at the Poperinge Hop Museum
new.desc: Poperinge is the heart of Belgium's hop country, and this museum in the old municipal weighing house tells the story of hop growing in the Westhoek. It also has a big collection of Belgian beers and ends with a tasting.
new.tip: It is open from late February to the end of November, closed on Mondays. A combined ticket with Talbot House is cheaper.

new.title: Go underground at the Memorial Museum Passchendaele 1917
new.desc: In the chateau grounds of Zonnebeke, this museum tells the story of the Battle of Passchendaele in 1917, in which about half a million men were killed or wounded for a few kilometres of mud. A reconstructed underground dugout and trench system lets you feel how soldiers lived.
new.tip: Combine it with Tyne Cot cemetery, a short drive or bike ride away. A family tour with a map and audio play keeps children engaged.

new.title: Walk the woods around Tillegem castle
new.desc: On the south-west edge of Bruges, the Tillegembos is a provincial woodland around a moated castle that was given its neo-Gothic look in the 19th century. The castle is now a provincial office, but the woods and meadows around it are open for walks.
new.tip: It is an easy bike ride from the centre. Follow the marked trails and look for the castle's reflection in the moat.

new.title: Explore the old heathland of Bulskampveld
new.desc: Bulskampveld near Beernem was once the largest medieval heathland in Flanders, about 10,000 hectares of heath, peat and fish ponds. Today the provincial domain around the 1893 castle covers some 230 hectares at the heart of the largest continuous forest in West Flanders.
new.tip: Follow one of the walking or cycling loops from the castle. It is quiet on weekdays, and a fine escape from crowded Bruges.

new.title: Meet the North Sea fish at Navigo in Oostduinkerke
new.desc: The National Fisheries Museum tells the story of the coast's fishermen and fisherwomen, from boys sailing to Iceland to fishing today. Its North Sea aquariums are a hit with children.
new.tip: The first Saturday of the month is free. Book tickets online, and pair the visit with the horseback shrimp fishers on the beach.

new.title: Find Dikke Mathille in Ostend's Leopoldpark
new.desc: Leopoldpark is the green heart of central Ostend, with ponds, old trees and a floral clock. Look for Dikke Mathille, the much-loved statue of a plump lady sunbathing.
new.tip: Bring a sandwich from town and sit by the water. It is a nice break between the beach and the shops.
